Recently, we have researched extensively, the difference and viability of information architectures, specifically, markdown, javascript and web technologies. This was, in it's most abstract, fundamental sense, a search for "Knowledge Navigation and Affordances in Technological space." Pushing the medium of the Computer to the absolute limits, to discover, in it's essence, how knowledge can be most effectively transported, transferred, recieved, understood, and hopefully; ethically integrated into action. That is something like a "Lifecycle and Telos of the Human pursuit of Knowledge."

Now, with that being said, the dramatic opening reveals a fascinating, simple discovery; One medium affords multiple views, while another begins from the assumption of a bias. (More on this later).

In essence, one of the most important properties in Computer Science, Math and even Linguistics itself; is Abstraction. Specifically, the Human ability to extract detail from a complex scene, and essentially "summarize" the whole. Extracting the invariants (to some degree), reducing resolutions of detail, while maintining the truthfulness of the original model(s).

However, in CS and Math, Abstraction is even more fundametnal; I think this concept is known as "Dynamic view, Source data." Where we begin with a primitive prototype base, and apply further abstractions and inherited properties from the prototype. Essentially, increasing capabilities of parts while building a hierarchy (or similar structure) of evolution.

This results in a fascinating emergent property; Inheritance. Why is inheritance so impotant? In the context of this research, it was the invariant of the problem; deciding whether to commit to one medium or another, to scale properly according to the necessities and purposes of the project (which is it's Telos.) In this sense, when we abstract the technologies, schema, archtiecture, scaling problems and even the knowledge, we are left with the abstractions; the few invariants that we the Human being can process. In this case:

- 1: Input (Low-level: knowledge)
- 2: Process (Firmware (so-to-speak): author, code, medium)
- 3: Output (High-level: view, web application, interaction, etc.).
	
This is where Abstraction and Inheritance...
    

However...I don't think Grammatica, or Research, or any methodology would replace the very act of Tangible experimentation (which is a fascinating concept for it's own discussion...)... in this case, experience with markdown, obsidian, filesystems, web technologies and general knowledge infrastructure, is the sample data; and that is the kind of data that is experiential; only discovered on-field. This suggests an idea; "Some paths are only revealed or known by the very act of walking them."

This means that Methodologies like Research, (and projects like Grammatica) serve even more tactile roles. Which suggests a general lifecycle of Methodology... each Domain of inquiry or problem sets, naturally afford specific instrumentation. In this case, much of the instruments are Cognitive and Abstract... but in the Experiential case; Collecting sample data on-field always posits risk of some kind (however, this methodological concept is a discussion for another day.)

In conclusion, one medium (markdown) affords multiple interpretations, while other mediums (jsx, js wiki api, zettelkasten, etc.) each assume a later stage in the ontology of systems (each are considerably more opinionated as compared to markdown or plaintext, and as such, each are naturally a bias.)

This means; one medium can be projected into dynamic, multiple interpretations, which was the primary problem (emphasis on this! This is the central gravity of the research and thesis.) Note: I am not sure if this kind of Reasoning or Methodology is "Heuristic" in Albert Simon's sense...

In this case, there are many problems that can be solved, by knowing which parts of a system can abstract into inherited implementation and interpretation... (this is how programming classes work, and it's how mathematics inherits abstractions from arithmetic to build further progressions, and it's also how linguistics works.) However, that is definitely a case for something like Grammatica, which is being developed specifically to solve these kinds of Topology problems, before deep committment into implementation or design...

This is precisely the tension point; when does one test ideas on-field, and when is abstract methodology (grammatica, research, schematics, etc.) the proper solution to complex problems?

That is worth researching!
